Tuberculosis (TB)
A Public Health Awareness Reference
For community health awareness use • Simple language for rural readers
Overview
Tuberculosis, commonly called TB, is a disease caused by germs (bacteria) called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It most often affects the lungs, but it can also affect other parts of the body such as the bones, kidneys, brain, or lymph nodes. TB spreads through the air when a person with active TB disease in the lungs coughs, sneezes, or speaks. It does not spread by sharing food, water, utensils, or by touching someone. Not everyone who breathes in TB germs becomes sick — many people carry the germs in an inactive form without any symptoms and cannot spread it to others. Only when the germs become active does a person develop TB disease and become infectious. TB is both preventable and curable. With early diagnosis and a complete course of treatment, almost all people with TB can be fully cured. Delaying treatment increases the risk of the disease spreading to family members and worsening the patient's health.
Common Symptoms
TB should be suspected when a person has any of the following symptoms, especially if they last more than two to three weeks:
Cough lasting more than two weeks, which may bring up mucus or blood
Fever, especially low-grade fever that continues for many days
Night sweats
Unexplained weight loss
Loss of appetite
Ongoing tiredness or weakness
Chest pain, particularly with breathing or coughing
Swelling in the neck or elsewhere, if TB affects the lymph nodes
Symptoms can develop slowly and may be mild at first, which is why people sometimes delay seeking care. Any person with a persistent cough of two weeks or more should get tested for TB.
Causes
TB is caused by infection with TB bacteria and spreads person to person through the air. Key points about how it spreads and who is at higher risk:
TB spreads when an infectious person coughs, sneezes, or speaks and releases germs into the air, which another person then breathes in
Close, prolonged contact with someone who has active lung TB — such as living in the same household — increases the risk of infection
Crowded or poorly ventilated living and working spaces make it easier for TB to spread
People with weaker immune systems are at higher risk of developing TB disease after infection, including those living with HIV, people with diabetes, people who are malnourished, and people who use tobacco or alcohol heavily
Children, elderly people, and those with chronic illness are more vulnerable to severe disease
It is important to remember that TB is a curable illness caused by germs — it is not caused by any curse, sin, or personal failing, and people with TB should not be shunned or discriminated against.
When to See a Doctor — Red Flag Signs
Visit the nearest government health centre, ASHA worker, or hospital for TB testing without delay if you or a family member has any of the following:
Cough lasting two weeks or more
Blood in sputum (coughed-up mucus)
Fever that continues for more than two weeks, especially with night sweats
Unexplained weight loss or ongoing loss of appetite
Chest pain along with cough or breathing difficulty
Persistent tiredness and weakness that does not improve with rest
A known close contact (family member or household member) recently diagnosed with TB, even without symptoms yet
Children with poor weight gain, prolonged fever, or swelling in the neck glands
Difficulty breathing or coughing up blood in large amounts — seek emergency care immediately
TB testing (such as sputum tests and chest X-ray) and treatment are available free of cost at government TB centres and health facilities. Do not wait for symptoms to worsen — early testing leads to faster cure and stops the disease from spreading to others.
Home Care and Prevention
Care during TB treatment
Take the full course of treatment exactly as advised by the health worker or doctor, even after feeling better — stopping early can make the disease harder to cure and can lead to drug-resistant TB.
Attend all follow-up visits and tests as scheduled.
Eat a nutritious diet with enough protein, fruits, and vegetables, as advised by the health worker, to support recovery.
Get adequate rest, especially in the early weeks of treatment.
Cover the mouth and nose with a cloth or mask while coughing or sneezing, and dispose of used tissues safely.
Keep the room well ventilated by opening windows and doors to let in fresh air and sunlight.
Avoid alcohol and tobacco use during treatment, as these can affect recovery.
Do not stop or change medicines without consulting the treating doctor or health worker.
Family members and close contacts should also get screened for TB, especially if they develop any symptoms.
Prevention
Ensure infants receive the BCG vaccine, which is given under the national immunisation programme and helps protect young children from severe forms of TB.
Keep living and working spaces well ventilated with good airflow and sunlight.
Avoid crowded, poorly ventilated spaces where possible, especially if someone nearby has an active cough.
Maintain good nutrition, as undernourishment increases the risk of developing TB disease.
If living with someone who has TB, follow the health worker's advice on precautions and get screened as a household contact.
Complete any preventive treatment recommended by a health worker for people at higher risk, such as household contacts or people living with HIV.
Seek prompt testing and treatment for anyone with prolonged cough or other symptoms — early treatment protects the whole family and community.
Odisha-Specific Notes
Odisha implements the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), including special campaigns to find and treat TB early, with particular attention to tribal, mining, and hard-to-reach districts of the state.
Free TB testing, chest X-ray, and treatment are available at government health facilities across Odisha, including Sub-Centres, Primary Health Centres (PHCs), Community Health Centres (CHCs), and District TB Centres.
The State TB Cell, under the Directorate of Public Health, Department of Health & Family Welfare, Government of Odisha, coordinates TB screening campaigns across all districts, including door-to-door and camp-based screening drives.
Odisha has several tribal-dominated and mining districts identified as high priority under the national programme; residents of these areas are encouraged to get screened promptly if symptoms appear, as access to care can be more limited in remote pockets.
Community volunteers called Ni-kshay Mitras provide nutritional and other support to TB patients and their families in Odisha as part of the Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan.
Patients registered for treatment may be eligible for a monthly nutritional support benefit under the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana, transferred directly to their bank account.
Contact your nearest ASHA worker, ANM, Sub-Centre, or PHC for free TB screening, or call the Odisha health helpline in case of doubt or difficulty accessing care.
India's TB Elimination Program
India runs the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, working towards the goal of eliminating TB ahead of global timelines. The Ni-kshay portal is the national system used by health workers to register TB patients, track testing and treatment, and connect patients with support services. Under this programme and related initiatives such as the Pradhan Mantri TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, testing and treatment for TB are provided completely free of cost at government health facilities, and additional nutritional and community support is available to registered patients through schemes like the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana and community volunteers known as Ni-kshay Mitras. Anyone with TB symptoms is encouraged to visit their nearest government health facility for free testing and care.
Source Basis
This document is based on general public health guidance and awareness materials from the World Health Organization (WHO), India's Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW) and National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP), the National Health Mission (NHM), and the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR). Content has been paraphrased and simplified for general community awareness; it does not reproduce any source text directly and does not cite specific studies or documents.
